title: CESTAT Quashes ₹46.41 Crore Service Tax Demand Against Yash Raj Films Over Overseas Shoots
meta_description: CESTAT Mumbai sets aside a ₹46.41 crore service tax demand on Yash Raj Films, holding its overseas line producers acted only as intermediaries.
court: Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, West Zonal Bench, Mumbai
bench: S.K. Mohanty (Judicial Member) and M.M. Parthiban (Technical Member)
case_name: Yashraj Films Private Limited v. Commissioner of CGST and Central Excise
citation: CESTAT Mumbai, Final Order (neutral citation and appeal number not available in public reporting); impugned Order-in-Original dated 14 December 2022
body: Film production houses that shoot abroad routinely hire local fixers to arrange crew, equipment, locations and permissions on the ground, and the tax department has long treated payments to such fixers as payments for an independent production service received from outside India, taxable in the recipient's hands under the reverse charge mechanism. The Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal's Mumbai bench has now told the department that this reading does not hold up where the overseas party was acting only as a facilitator, setting aside a demand of over Rs 46 crore against Yash Raj Films.

The dispute covered the period from April 2013 to June 2017 and involved payments Yash Raj Films made to overseas Local Area Representatives, sometimes called line producers, engaged for shooting assistance on films including Dhoom 3, Gunday and Befikre. The department's case, recorded in an Order-in-Original dated December 14, 2022, was that these Local Area Representatives supplied an independent film-production service from outside India, so that Yash Raj Films, as the Indian recipient, owed service tax on a reverse charge basis. The order confirmed a demand of Rs 46,40,92,070, along with interest, a penalty of an equal amount under Section 78 of the Finance Act, 1994, and a further penalty of Rs 10,000 under Section 77(2).

Before the Tribunal, Yash Raj Films argued that its Local Area Representatives were nothing more than intermediaries. Their job was to arrange local facilities, personnel and other logistical requirements for the overseas shoot, while every creative, budgetary and business decision connected with the film remained with Yash Raj Films itself. On that analysis, the Local Area Representatives were not providing the main production service on their own account; they were merely helping Yash Raj Films procure services from third parties on the ground. That distinction matters because an intermediary's service is treated as provided at the intermediary's own location, which in this case was outside India, taking the transaction outside the reach of the reverse charge mechanism altogether.

The bench of S.K. Mohanty and M.M. Parthiban accepted this framing. Examining the production agreements on record, the Tribunal found that the Local Area Representatives' role was ancillary and confined to facilitation, arranging crew, equipment and permissions, rather than producing any part of the film on their own account. Since Yash Raj Films retained full control over the creative and commercial aspects of production, the Local Area Representatives fell squarely within the description of an intermediary rather than an independent service provider.

That finding was enough to dispose of the entire demand. If the Local Area Representatives were intermediaries, the place of provision of their service was their own location abroad, and Yash Raj Films had no reverse charge liability to discharge on payments made to them. The Tribunal accordingly set aside the Rs 46.41 crore demand in full, along with the associated interest and both penalties.

For production houses and media companies that route international shoots through local representatives abroad, the ruling draws a workable line between a genuine production service received from overseas and mere local facilitation paid for by an Indian producer. Where the Indian company keeps control over the creative and commercial decisions, and the overseas party's role is limited to arranging people, equipment and permissions on the ground, that arrangement reads as intermediation rather than an independent taxable service, and reverse charge should not apply. Production houses with similar overseas shooting arrangements from the service tax era, and under the analogous place-of-supply rules now in force under GST, would do well to review their contracts against this distinction before the department raises a fresh round of demands on the same facts.

The ruling also illustrates how far back service tax litigation still runs. A demand covering transactions from 2013 to 2017, confirmed only in December 2022, took until October 2026 to be finally set aside at the first appellate forum, a reminder that reverse charge disputes tied to cross-border production arrangements from the pre-GST years remain very much alive before the tribunals.
why_it_matters: The ruling gives Indian production houses a concrete test for when an overseas line producer counts as a mere intermediary rather than an independent service provider: retained creative and commercial control by the Indian company points toward intermediation, which falls outside reverse charge. Companies facing similar demands over cross-border shoot arrangements, whether under the old service tax regime or today's GST place-of-supply rules, can use this reasoning to contest reverse charge assessments on facilitation payments to overseas representatives.
card_summary: CESTAT Mumbai quashes a ₹46.41 crore reverse-charge service tax demand on Yash Raj Films, holding its overseas line producers were intermediaries, not independent production-service providers.
card_tip: If your overseas shoot representative only arranges local crew and permissions while you keep creative and commercial control, that is intermediation, not a taxable import of service.
verification_notes: The demand figure (Rs 46,40,92,070), impugned Order-in-Original date (14 December 2022), dispute period (April 2013-June 2017), the films named, the penalties under Sections 78 and 77(2), the bench composition, and the intermediary-based reasoning are corroborated across LiveLaw Biz and TaxGuru's independent reports. Taxsutra's case listing independently confirms the ruling and bench. Sources differ slightly on the precise order date, LiveLaw Biz's report is dated 17 October 2026 while Taxsutra's listing records 21 October 2026; this report uses the earlier, more directly sourced date and flags the discrepancy rather than asserting either as certain. The appeal number and a formal neutral citation were not available in any source checked and have accordingly been left out rather than invented.
